title: How the 100x plugin works, end to end

subject.lede: 100x is a Claude Code plugin that turns a plain-English request into verified work. Think of it as a building with a front desk: the router skill is the receptionist who works out what you need, skills are the rulebooks each department follows, agents are the specialists who do the work in parallel, tools are the measuring instruments, and hooks are the security guards at the doors who check a signed receipt before anything leaves the building.

tldr.what: It routes any engineering request to the right rulebooks and specialist agents, and refuses to call work done until a check has really passed.
tldr.how: A front-door skill picks the plan, agents do the work, a separate verifier re-runs the checks and signs a receipt, and guards at commit time read that receipt.
tldr.watch_out: The guards only block in a repository that turns them on; everywhere else they just warn.

context.purpose: Anyone joining the project, or using the plugin for the first time, can see what each part is for and follow one request from the moment it is typed to the moment it is committed.
context.why_now: The plugin has grown to {{skills}}, {{agents}} and {{tools}}; a newcomer needs the map before the parts make sense.

entry_points.label: bin dispatcher: <tool> [args]
entry_points.note: every tool runs through one dispatcher; the build walkthrough calls several

entry_points.label: git commit / push / gh pr create

terms.means: A rulebook in skills/<name>/SKILL.md that Claude loads for one kind of task. Each rule says what enforces it.
terms.example: bug-fix: reproduce first, commit the failing test, then fix.

terms.means: The front-door skill, invoked by the plugin's own name as a slash command. It names the kind of request, asks only questions that change the plan, and picks the skills and agents.
terms.example: "add an export endpoint" is a build.

terms.means: A specialist sub-session defined in agents/<name>.md, with its own tools and preloaded skills.
A Python script in scripts/ run through the single dispatcher in bin/. Tools check things a rule can only ask for.
A script Claude Code runs on an event (session start, before a shell command, at the end of a turn). It can add context, ask, or block.
terms.example: Before git commit, check the receipt.

terms.means: plan.json: the tasks of one feature, who owns which files, what each depends on, and which commands verify it.
terms.example: T1 backend owns src/api/**; T2 frontend depends on T1.

terms.means: A group of tasks with no ordering between them and no shared files, so they can run at the same time.
The JSON block an agent ends with: what it changed, the commands it ran and their exit codes, and its status.
Re-running the verify commands the plan declared for a task, instead of believing the exit codes in the report.
A file written by the verified tool after a check passes, signed with a private key and tied to the exact content of your files.
A hash of every tracked file's content. Change one byte and it changes, so an old receipt no longer matches.
A second checkout of the same repository in its own folder, so two agents edit files without stepping on each other.

outline.title: route(request): the router skill, as pseudocode

lines.code: intent, tier = classify(request)   # build, fix, incident, understand, …
plan = stamp(plan_json); plan_dag.lint(plan)   # cycles, shared files, unowned ACs
for wave in waves(plan): run one agent per task, own worktree

outline.title: require_verification(command): the commit gate, as pseudocode

lines.code: if not in_a_git_repo: return allow            # nothing to gate
if policy is None: return warn("not configured")
if no receipt: return deny("run the checks first")
fresh = [c for c in receipt if c.fingerprint == fingerprint(files)]
if required check not fresh: return deny("re-run verification")
return pass                                   # no 'allow': your own ask rules still apply

scenarios.title: A build request, from typing it to committing it

steps.t: The session starts and a hook points Claude at the router
steps.d: With dozens of skills installed the menu gets cut off, so a hook injects a short reminder to start with the router.

steps.t: You type a request in plain English
steps.d: Any wording works; the example request is made up.

steps.t: The router names the kind of work and asks a few questions
steps.d: It says "this is a build", the scale tier, and asks at most {{questions}}, only ones whose answer changes the plan, each with a recommendation.

steps.t: The router loads the skills for a build, in order
steps.d: Requirements intake, feature planning, then per-area rulebooks such as API contract and data modelling, then code craft and review.

steps.t: The plan becomes a task graph and a tool checks it
steps.d: Before any agent starts, the graph is checked for loops, two tasks owning the same file, and requirements nobody owns.

steps.t: Two agents pick up a wave in parallel, each in its own worktree
steps.d: Each agent is a specialist with its own preloaded skills; separate worktrees keep their edits apart.

steps.t: The agents edit files and send their reports
steps.d: A report lists the files changed and the commands run with exit codes. It is a claim, not proof.

steps.t: The main session checks each report against git and replays the checks
steps.d: It asks git which files really changed, rejects any outside the task's owned files, and re-runs only the verify commands the plan declared.

steps.t: A separate verifier agent re-runs everything itself
steps.d: It trusts no report and never fixes what it finds, so the party doing the work is not the party grading it.

steps.t: The check passes and a signed receipt is written for these exact files
steps.d: The receipt holds a fingerprint of the file contents, signed with a key only this machine has.

steps.t: You commit, and the commit guard reads the receipt
steps.d: The receipt's fingerprint matches the files, so the guard steps aside. It never says allow, so your own permission rules still apply.

steps.t: The turn ends and a stop hook asks for one second look
steps.d: Blind runs found a second skeptical pass catches defects the first missed, so a long or file-editing turn is held once with a re-check prompt.

scenarios.title: What if the session believed the agent's report?

steps.t: One agent also edits a shared file it does not own, and skips the tests
steps.d: Its report still says done, tests pass. Nothing in the report itself is false-looking.

steps.t: The session takes the report at its word and merges
do: nobody ran the tests on this content

steps.t: A broken change lands, and it collides with the other agent's work

scenarios.title: Fix: check the report against git, then replay the declared checks

steps.t: The report is compared with what git says changed
steps.d: The shared file is outside the task's owned files, so the report is rejected before anything runs.

steps.t: The plan's own verify commands are re-run, not the report's
steps.d: Commands in a report are text another agent wrote, so only the plan's declared ones run.

steps.t: The task goes back to its agent with the reason
do: nothing merged; the agent sees the failing command

scenarios.title: What if the receipt were only a "tests passed" flag?

steps.t: Checks pass and a receipt is recorded
Claude makes one more small edit after verifying
steps.d: A typo fix, a renamed variable: the kind of change nobody re-tests. The receipt now describes content that no longer exists.

steps.t: The commit only asks whether a receipt exists
steps.d: A pass or fail flag cannot tell old content from new. The real receipt stores a fingerprint with each check, which is what the fix compares.

steps.t: Code nobody tested is committed

scenarios.title: Fix: the receipt is tied to a fingerprint of the files

steps.t: The commit guard compares the receipt's fingerprint with the files now
steps.d: They differ, so the guard denies the commit and prints the command to re-run.
do: deny: receipt is for other content

steps.t: Claude re-runs the check, which writes a fresh receipt
The commit is tried again and goes through

options.label: Instructions only: tell the model to verify before saying done
cons: A model can talk itself past prose
No proof the check ran on the content that ships

options.label: Rely on CI after push
cons: Feedback comes after the push, not before
Does not stop a turn that just says done

options.label: Signed, content-bound receipt checked by hooks at commit, push and stop
pros: Editing after verifying invalidates the proof
Fails open, so a broken guard never locks the shell
cons: Only blocks where a policy file turns it on
Not a defence against an agent set on defeating it

decision.deciding_factor: The check has to happen before the work leaves the machine and be tied to the exact content, which only a fingerprinted, signed receipt read by a hook gives.
decision.revisit_when: Claude Code gains a built-in, tamper-evident verification step, or CI becomes fast enough to run before every commit.

checks.q: The agents say "tests pass". What does the main session do before believing it?
checks.answer: Asks git which files really changed, rejects anything outside the task's owned files, and re-runs the plan's own verify commands.

checks.q: A receipt exists. Should the commit go through?
checks.answer: Not yet: the receipt is for the old content. Only a fingerprint comparison can tell, which is the fix.

checks.q: What will the guard say this time?
checks.answer: Nothing in the way: the fresh receipt matches the files, so it steps aside.
